title: The DiCecco Daily Special: Former Eagles TE Cornelius Ingram Turned Bitterness Into Something Better
text: [music] >> Hello and welcome into another episode of the Check-Out Daily, but it's a special edition of the Check-Out Daily because we're kick-starting our Where Are They Now series for Inside the Birds. And our first guest was a fifth-round pick of the Philadelphia Eagles in 2009, the 153rd pick to be exact. And that is former Eagles tight end Cornelius Ingram who's kind enough to give me a few minutes. Cornelius, how are you doing, man? >> I'm doing great. Doing great. Uh thanks for having me on. >> Absolutely. So, you're from Hawthorne, uh Florida. And >> Yep. >> it had to be special for you to go to the University of Florida, but what were some of the other options that you had and what led you to choosing to be a Gator? >> Yeah, uh I'm coming out of high school. Um I I went to a course Hawthorne. And we were middle school through high school. So, you know, the the middle schoolers we were walking the campus with the high schoolers, but I had an advantage as a as a seventh-grader. I moved up on varsity and played basketball. So, um I was able to start my my recruiting process a little earlier than a lot of, you know, normal high school kids. And University of Florida, you know, they took notice as an eighth-grader um for for for me. So, I don't want to say it was a no-brainer because when you go through the recruiting process, of course, um there's other coaches at other colleges that you you end up having a great relationship with, of course. Um you might fall in love with scheme, system, whatever the case may be. Um and I I I felt that way going through my recruiting process. So, um was recruited I was recruited by a lot of schools in both sports. And um of course, you know, the University of Florida being 20 minutes away from Hawthorne, um everyone thought it was a no-brainer. Uh but to be honest, I went through the process where um I went on visits. Um of course, I had tons of home visits from from different colleges and coaches. And um I can remember on a couple home visits, my dad was always a die-hard Gator. So, uh I was recruited by Ron Zook at the time and then Billy Donovan was the basketball coach. And I can remember when when both of those coaches would come in for a home visit, right? My my dad, he wanted to throw a barbecue. He wanted to invite everyone over. Um but if it was like, let's say someone like Florida State with Bobby Bowden coming to Hawthorne and coming to the house to visit, my dad would basically shut down and stay in the room. So, I kind of I kind of knew, you know, um I had to be a Gator, you know, just because, you know, my dad wanted me to go there. But again, I I I I did form a great relationship with with the entire coaching staff. I think they recruited me the longest because I was right in the backyard. Um and my my career was was wonderful. I had a great career there. Um and I definitely made the right decision. >> Do you remember who hosted you on your recruiting visit at Florida? >> Uh Dallas Baker. >> Okay, wide receiver. >> Wide receiver. Yep, wide receiver. Um just talked to Dallas the other day. He's the receiver coach at at at Baylor. Um great great guy. Um yep, Dallas Bake- Dallas Baker hosted me. Um and I had a fun visit. >> Seems like the University of Florida and many colleges are like this, but it has a unique fraternity. Do you still keep in contact with a lot of the guys you played with? >> I do. I do. Um I have a couple uh group texts with with with some of the former players, my former teammates that that played there. I try to stay out the way even though I'm still in the backyard. I try to stay out the way. You know, because I you know, I know how how things go, but most of the time if if, you know, a couple of my former teammates would would would call and say, "Hey, we're going to be in town for this Gator game." Of course, we'll link up, but yeah, we do stay in contact. A lot of them are back here in Florida in the state of Florida. So, when they're spring football, of course, here is crazy. So, it's a big deal. So, a lot of people come back around whether they're at the spring game or just at practice, but definitely at home games. We stay in contact. Away games, we're always in our group chat talking about the game that we're watching when we're playing away. But yeah, I got a great relationship with with with a lot of the cats that I played with. >> Now, how did you go about balancing the you know, the weight training and the conditioning aspect being a two-sport athlete? I imagine that there were some conflicts at times. >> Yeah, no, it was tough. It was tough. I redshirted. I redshirted in football, you know, and that was a part of my recruiting process when I talked with every every college and every coach. You know, they knew being a two-sport athlete was something that I really really wanted to do. So, they were basically aware of where my heart was. So, I redshirted in football so I can just kind of focus on it was almost strictly basketball when I was doing basketball. But then there were sometimes where I had to do certain things with with the football team because you can't have two two So, one of the other sports, they have to offer you the other one, um you're a walk-on. So, I was basically a walk-on um because like I said, you can't have two two scholarships. And when when it was time to do certain things for football, I was obligated to do things for football because I was on a football scholarship, but um it was tough to do, of course. Um I I only end up doing it 1 year, but you know, it was a dream of mine to play two sports and I had that opportunity at one of the best schools there is. And um I will say this, I think I stopped playing basketball year two um too soon because the year after um they wanted two national championships. So, thank God I end up winning two national championships in football, um but if I would have kept playing basketball, I would have been a part of those national championship teams. >> And your son, CJ, is an electric player to watch. We'll get to him uh later in the later in the interview, but when you look at your you know, when you look back, do you feel like your basketball background really translated to the football field and specifically with tight ends? When you look at Antonio Gates and some players like that, um how how do you feel it really helped uh shape your game? >> A lot. A lot. Um I I know, you know, just being a a really good athlete um in in general, but when you're talking about hand-eye coordination, um footwork, uh because I was kind of like a big guard where I I would, you know, could play on the perimeter, um but I could post up smaller guards. Um and then and it definitely helped me move around on the football field. So, um of course now, whenever I, you know, just hear about, you know, football players with with with basketball backgrounds, um I kind of light up because I know how instrumental uh the basketball side of it it helps you extremely extremely a lot for for football as well. So, it definitely helped me. I'm glad I was able to do both. It was a dream of mine and I was able to live out my dream. >> And if I'm correct on this, you began practicing as a quarterback. >> Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Graduate left left high school as all American quarterback. I was a also Elite 11 quarterback. Oh, yes. I definitely had quarterback background in my game and when I went to Florida, I went there as a quarterback and then like I said earlier, you know, being recruited by you know, one coach and then when that coach leaves, right? Coach Meyer came in and he had his you know, his recruits that that he probably recruited when he was at Utah. [clears throat] At that time, I didn't understand how a lot of the things work, but but now of course, you know, seeing what's going on in in in in college football, even high school football now that I'm a head coach, I have a better understanding of you know, some guys followed that coach that recruited him. Doesn't matter if it's at that particular school or or or another. So, at that time, I didn't want to understand it, but now going through the process and not only as a player, but now as a coach as well, I have a great understanding of it. >> And so, what sparked the transition to tight end? >> Well, when when Coach Meyer came in, you know, I think Cam Newton, Tim Tebow, he had those guys. He were recruiting those guys at at other places and I was a really good athlete like I said. I'll be honest, you know, being in a small town, you know, I had a decent arm. I was tall, but deep down inside I knew I could play another position. So, once I made that transition, right, it was it was pretty smooth to be [clears throat] honest, right? I I wasn't really used to the contact as far as blocking at the tight end position, but once I switched over Coach Meyer made sure that transition was something where I can line up outside like a receiver. I wasn't known as a traditional tight end at that time. So, and and the game was changing anyway at that point in time. The game was changing. So, he used me at wide receiver more than anything. So, and I was able to, you know, let my natural ability athleticism take over out on the perimeter. Because again, I wasn't the traditional tight end. So, just Coach Meyer and them kind of having their own recruits, us kind of sitting down and talking, and and you could probably can attest to this, you know, back then, you know, regardless of, you know, where you thought about transferring to, no matter what, you were going to have to sit out a year. And I was coming off a redshirt freshman year. I was like, man, listen, I want to get on the field. I want to play. >> You were part of a national championship team at Florida, Cornelius. >> Mhm. >> You were really a key piece in the 2007 season. You were up for the John Mackey Award, which is a prestigious award that has, you know, the most prominent tight ends in college football. What was that experience like for you, that 2-year period? >> No, it was probably one of the best experiences I've had in my life. Um, you talking about, you know, a roster full of NFL potential from from the offensive side of the ball, the defensive side of the ball. A lot of the coaches that were on staff under Coach Meyer, you know, end up being head coaches at other universities years years and years afterwards. So, you know, I'm able to share, you know, you know, with my family these experiences. Not only that, but my players that I coach now about, you know, the times and and how things were at the University [clears throat] of Florida, right? And considering, right, national champions um in basketball. Like, all those guys were on campus at the same time. Um the baseball program was really good, the track program. So, uh the University of Florida at that time was probably the hottest uh university. And um I was able to, you know, play a part in and and a lot of it. Um I've I've created a lot of memories um with with with special teammates that that I I've grown to know even up until now. Um and it's one of the best things I ever experienced. Yep. >> And then, in terms of the health in a health perspective, you run into your first bout of adversity >> in 2008. That was supposed to be the perfect season for you segueing into the NFL. Not to dwell on it, but what are your recollections of that? >> You know, I think I think now, how how everything unfolded in in my life and then a lot of it, you know, came from the injury. It was a blessing in disguise, I think, for for for me when I first tore my ACL, right? You You're talking about someone who's never had a jam finger before. And um to tear my ACL going into my senior hardest thing I've ever had to deal with. And um you know, when I tore it in in practice, I think it was maybe the second day of training camp in practice, and I didn't even know it was it was torn at that time. I ended up finishing practice full speed. Once I got home uh and of course right shower, eating, do all these things and I I fell asleep and I remember waking up right in my my knee was about this big. And I remember calling the training staff and you know just telling them like hey, listen I need to come in right away. So I end up going to the practice facility like early the next morning just so right our team doctor and of course our trainers can can look at my knee and they was like hey listen we need to get a MRI and I'm like well I don't think it's that serious. So I go in to get my MRI and I get the MRI and I'm kind of waiting on the results and the doctor they're like stalling and um from from where I was seated uh waiting on the MRI results I could see outside of the building where uh the entranceway was right underneath me and I see like Urban Meyer car pull in, Dan Mullen car pull in, Charlie Strong and I'm looking at the time I'm like yo we should be in practice right now. And and uh you know these guys are pulling in here made me wonder and of course they wanted coach Meyer to come in and and break the news um and it was tough. Like I said I I never had a jammed finger before my entire high school career, college career and to to tear your ACL going into your senior season where right you got to have high expectations of course you're a key piece to to to the team um it was it was extremely tough. Um you know and I I I I'll be honest I got emotional um right away and then you know I gave it some time and after that you know I was just trying to refocus and um get myself prepared for the draft right because you know ACL injury of course full recovery time is a year you know so but it was tough it was tough I think you know just experiencing that and then maybe a couple more episodes pretty similar it prepared me for what I'm doing right now kidding or not >> When did you start to feel like yourself leading up to the draft process? >> Well I will say this I had I had a cadaver done for my first surgery and you can recover from that the fastest so maybe maybe five months out I think from early September to February I did everything full speed almost full speed at the draft which is you know kind of unusual and I I felt good you know I felt like I was at least 85% and I just wanted to show the NFL teams that you know I had fully recovered I felt great but it wasn't until like maybe a couple months after that where I felt probably 100% so never really um fully reach my potential of course you know going going through the injury of course once I got to Philly um you know I was one of the most talked about guys on the team I had a lot of success but really on in mini camp and training camp and then I re-tore the same ACL and you know it was it was it was very frustrating at that time only only because again right I'm thinking about in the past never had to deal with any injuries but my second my second injury was actually a blessing Dr. Andrews did the second surgery and um, I could remember when I woke up from surgery, my parents were on the other side of the glass, and right, my mom was super emotional. Um, my dad, he was trying to keep it together, and um, Dr. Andrews started explaining. He was like, "Listen, um, the the cadaver um, was it just it it it it failed, and it was it just about to it was going to start to rot in my leg, where, you know, it could have got infected, could have got in my bloodstream, where I could have had my leg amputated, or I could have died from it. You know, and this was the second surgery. So, um, it was it was truly a blessing. Of course, I love the game of football. Um, I love being around it, right? But, but, but, I love life a little bit more. So, even though I wasn't able to do what I wanted to do at that particular time, um, my second ACL tear was actually a a a blessing for me going forward. >> And would that have been August 2009, or something somewhere around >> Yep. Yep. Yep. Following year. Yep. Following year. Mhm. >> Wow. So, do you I know that we're I recognize we're going back a number of years, but do you have any recollection as to how that injury transpired? Were you running a route? Was it non-contact? >> Um, I will say this. I think I think even at the NFL combine, I remember uh, Drew Rosenhaus was my agent, and he was like, "Listen, a lot of the teams, they still like you, but they, you know, some of their team doctors feel like there's there's something, you know, funny going on." I was like, "Well, I still feel fine. I felt I felt good, um, honestly speaking." So, I I I really didn't really didn't know. I think the graft, right? It it it probably ran its ran its course. Um, now, I will say this. I was kind of unaware of you know, using a cadaver, um not knowing that uh I think the first thing I heard was if you use the cadaver, right, this is the surgery that you can recover from the fastest. Right, let's go, you know, cuz right I'm thinking about my future, you know, I was ready to hit the panic button cuz again, you're talking about going back to school where uh you know, I was considering leaving my junior year. Um I was considering leaving my junior year, then you go back to school to to have a season-ending injury, right, of course you feel devastated. So, uh I think it just it just ran it ran its course. Um nothing in particular in practice that I felt like I was doing. I will say this, I think the Eagles did a unbelievable job with like just rehabbing me. There were there were sometimes where um I was I was limited in reps. Um and I and I felt good after my first surgery coming out of Florida, but uh after we found out it was torn the second time, again, the the the the whole timing of it was was was perfect for me because like I said, Dr. Andrews felt like maybe a day or two later right, it would have been really bad. um I'm extremely blessed um to be here, of course, and uh I've had lots of success after that. I can say that. >> Now, when that happened, Cornelius, was there ever any doubt that crept in knowing that that was the second time that you torn uh your ACL and your trajectory was trending upwards, and I imagine that the frustration was really settling in. >> It was. It was. Again, you know, I just I just felt like you know, it was it was my time. I felt like it was my time, and and and everything was pointing towards, you know, me having success, me getting on the field, me playing. And then, yeah, when when when it happened, right, of course, right, certain things play out in your head, right, you feel you feel a certain way about it. And I was still trying to maintain. I ended up in Denver. Like, I was I was still trying to maintain, never really fully recovered. And um when I was completely when I was completely finished, I was like, "You know what? I don't want to go through this anymore. You know, let's just, you know, figure out what's the next step." I stopped watching football for a while. Stopped watching football for a while because, you know, I would I would I would get emotional. You know, I've always supported my teammates or or or friends that that I had who who still continued their career, of course. Um but it was it was extremely hard to watch the game because I always just felt like it should have been me, right? It should have been me. And you know, I always feel, you know, my players now, right, and and they're so young and they don't understand, right? I found my purpose. I found my purpose now, the the the the way I ended up back in my hometown coaching high school football. I found my my my purpose. And when you find your purpose and you're walking through it, I really just feel like there's a lot of success for you on the other side. And I've been able I've been able to do that. I think maybe what, 12 years now I've been a high school head coach. And it's been phenomenal. >> So, that's a perfect segue. At what point did you realize I'm good. I'm I I'm I'm going to turn the page and and move on to the next chapter. And how did you find your calling ultimately? >> Well, the calling actually found me. >> [laughter] >> My calling actually found me and I I I didn't know it at that time. Uh our principal and our athletic director at Hawthorne, you know, they they came to me about being the head coach. And coaching never was even on my radar. You know, I was kind of traveling, doing my own thing, you know, like coaching was never on my radar. So, I can remember when they first um addressed me with it. Uh initially, I said no right away and the AD and the principal, they were pretty persistent. They came back at the end of the week. And then they had something else to offer as well. They was like, "Well, listen, the school you graduated from, we're on the verge of shutting down." Right? Uh my my former high school was a D-letter grade for like 2 years in a row and the state was ready to shut the school down. And honest to God, that's how I got into coaching. Wasn't ready. I didn't even know exactly where to start. Um the year prior to me taking the job, there were 15, 16 players on the team. Right? Of course, there were no money in the football account. It was in the negative. Right? So, the job wasn't appealing at all. And and like I said, the school was also a D-letter grade. they just felt like I would be able to give the school a spark some kind of way. Um of course, through football. And man, when I said yes, I never looked back. When I said yes to taking the job, I never looked back. You know, just alone my first my first team meeting, right? It was almost 60 guys who showed up. And I was like, "Man, there was 16 guys on the team last year, so you're telling me we have these kids in the school, right? They just They They just didn't want to play football. It was a bad time, not even just the year before, but I think maybe a couple years before that we were the laughing stock of high school football in the state of Florida. And um again, I I just kind of stepped out on faith, wanted to help my former high school um get over that hump, not only academically, but of course athletically as well. And And I kid you not, we've been able to do it. We've been able to do it. >> Hey Philly fans, game day is stressful enough. Parking, traffic, long lines. We've all been there. But when it comes to your cannabis, Camden Apothecary makes it easy. This is the dispensary for sports fans. Just minutes outside of Philly with plenty of free parking, you'll be in and out fast, no hassle, no waiting. And they don't just care about convenience. Camden Apothecary is all about the guest experience. Their staff makes sure you feel taken care of every time you walk in. Plus, they carry only the best quality cannabis at the fairest prices. So, whether you're stocking up for the tailgate, the watch party, or celebrating a big win, you know you're getting the good stuff without overpaying. They even show love to the community with specials for fans, students, service members, and healthcare pros. Camden Apothecary, top quality cannabis, great prices, and an experience made for Philly fans 21 and up. >> You mentioned that coaching never entered your mind previously, and you've played the game your whole life, but I imagine it's different when you're in that seat. So, how long did it take you to really establish your voice and and your and establish your messaging? >> Um probably maybe 2 years in. I think maybe 2 years in um I was able to kind of, you know, figure some things out. I I think for me, I've always been an open book, right? I would, you know, call other coaches. I would pick their brains, of course. Um my older brother, he was actually the head boys basketball coach at that time. Um he was the offensive coordinator for for the football team. So, uh we would always talk about, you know, new things we wanted to try. Um maybe, you know, go a different route with this or that. And and he would give me some advice. Um I can remember when I first took the job, um Urban Meyer, he was at Ohio State. And he he owned the lake house right outside of Hawthorne. So, he invited me to his house. I think they were about to play Alabama in the national championship. And and he was home for like a week. So, he invited me over for dinner. And after dinner, we we we we talked for a while. And I can remember, right? It's probably some of the best advice I've received going into my coaching career. He said, "Listen, whatever you do, you hire you hire some stand-up guys. And you let them do their job. Right? You don't have to coach every position. Right? You don't have to right, run the special teams, run the defense, run the offense. You let them do their job." And I I took that in consideration, of course. and he's he's always sup- supported me, even now. But but I thought that was huge because in my mind going into it, I was thinking exactly that. Listen, I have to do everything. I have to control everything. And I I I was extremely happy when I when I heard it from, of course, one of the greatest um to to to let let your coaches do their job. Let them coach. Um, hold their position group accountable. And I I've been able to use a lot of those different methods. Um, and I I put them into my coaching style, of course. And I've had success doing it. I've had success doing it. >> Well, how what kind of coach would you classify yourself as? Someone who's sort of old school, like a Vic Fangio, or you're more of a players players type of coach? >> a mixture So, I'm a mixture of it all, right? I I think for for for me, I'm pretty I'm pretty firm with my guys. Um, I'm not that old, so I know what they're listening to. When we work out, right? Normally, I'm the DJ. Uh, or if they're the if if or if I let players, you know, control the music, they know, you know, there's at least three, four songs I want to hear. Um, and and and we make sure everyone has different variety of music that they want to listen to. Um, it's it's a it's a great feel. I have a little old school in me. I yell some. I do yell some. I I I challenge my guys every single day. I'm talking about on and off the field. And and I'll be completely honest, I didn't know if that style would really work. Um, especially with this generation. Um, because again, I'm not that old, but you know, some of my coaches that that I've had, whether they're, you know, college coaches or especially high school coaches, right? They were hands-on and they were old school guys. And and there was no way around it, right? What you see is what you get. But but I have a little mixture of everything and and in my coaching style. And I say this to to a lot of people. I'm going into year 12. I've never been disrespected as a as a head coach. Not one time, right? I've had some big-time players come through my program. Um I've had kids with, you know, bad home situations. Like regardless, right? We try to we we we try to help our players out as much as possible. Um I have this open-door policy. Um my players know when I'm not at the school, and that's if my office door is closed. Every single day my office door is wide is is wide open because, you know, there's a lot that that that goes goes on now in in society. A lot of these kids need that outlet, and I didn't want to be that mean coach who who who never wanted to relate to the kids, never wanted to, you know, I just hold a conversation with a kid, right? I'm able to talk about any and everything um with my players. When they go out to school, as soon as they come back, they they they stop by. Um what I think the last 6 years we've been in the state championship game, and we've won three of those, right? I have kids that Division Ones, Division Twos, Juco, right? To see where our program um is now, right? It speaks volumes to not not only myself, but the amazing coaches I have around me, the caliber of players that that that we're around every single day. And I think probably the most important thing um for me is these parents allow me to coach their kids um a lot different than some other coaches. I'll be honest. And it And it might have And it might And it might have a lot to do with me coaching at home. Right? I I know a lot of these kids. I grew up with their parents or some some relative, and I think, you know, just that alone helps me with the way I coach. >> What's your perspective on the future of Hawthorne football and your role in that? >> Well, I'm offered jobs every year. >> I'm offered jobs every every year, whether it's college level, um, course, high school level. You know, I want things to be intact. I'll be honest. I know I won't be there forever, but I want things to be be intact because right, this is this is a place I call home. Um, and and and for us, um, I probably should have mentioned this earlier, right, we we play top-notch competition and we're probably the smallest school in the entire state of Florida. And I I I take my hat off to my players every single day. Like today, we just had we we we we work out Monday through Thursday, um, and we just had a great day today and I was talking with one of my coaches on the way home just raving about how good, you know, our lift ended up and then we we go outside and we condition. But my my kids aren't entitled. They're not entitled, right? I wish you can fly down and see our facilities. I wish you can, you know, fly down and see what we have to work with. And for us to have, uh, limited resources with the type of success we've had, my kids don't care. As long as I show up, me and my coaching staff, they will be [snorts] there. They don't care about field turf. They don't care about raggedy equipment, whether it's in the weight room, whether it's shoulder pads, right? We're doing a lot of stuff with less. But but when I tell you this, when my kids graduate from high school, um, they're ready to go take on whatever the world has to offer for them. And they they're they're they're not perfect, but right if a supervisor or a boss yell or challenge them at work, they're not walk walking off their job. You know, um a lot of my players that are still playing college ball, right they come back and we talk like, "Coach, I laugh at my position coach because right you said you know, maybe worse things. >> But but it was only to challenge them. I have to push buttons. I have to figure out, you know, how to get how to how to motivate you or figure out how can you make this play? Um how can you give me your all and right and I feel like it's my job to have these kids not only prepare for college football, but for the real world because right we both know how hard it is. So, um again, we we get to do this um with with with limited resources than a lot of schools. I'm talking about a lot of schools. So, um that's why it's hard for me to leave. I'll be honest, it's hard for me to leave and I'm talking for the last 8 years I've could have had numerous of of, you know, head coaching jobs in in in in in these high-paying states like Georgia and Alabama. Um Florida being one of probably the lowest paying coaching uh state there is. Right, it's all about home for me. Um a lot of these kids they don't have father figures. A lot of these kids they don't have a positive role model. Again, I I I I always think about how bitter I was towards the game and not being able to finish my career the way I wanted wanted and to have the type of success I've had as a coach. Right, this is I mean it's it's it sounds like right we're probably writing a script for for a Netflix uh documentary or something, but these are all facts, man. To to be able to live out this in my hometown means almost everything to me. Heck, man, I can go on. Man, I have a street named after me, Arthur Warren. Uh I I should have said this as well. I was the girls basketball coach. Um I have three state titles in girls basketball. And with the all the all of this is like in the last five, six years. Right? Three in girls basketball, three in football. Our boys have, I think, two or three state titles in the last two or three uh the last five, six years. Which my older brother, like I said, is still the head boys coach. So, to have all this success at these smallest school, probably financially, the town is probably, you know, one of those towns where, right, there's not that many local businesses that can help us out financially. Right? You got to think, we need new equipment. We have to pay for state championship rings. With all this stuff going on around us, right, our kids, you know, they they they they really work extremely hard. Um I feel like I have a dream job now, and I know the football gods blessed me after my injury to to be able to be back home and have this amount of success. >> And what's really special about your story is that you said you walked away from the game feeling bitter, but you've grown into this role and have embraced it, and now you get to sort of live vicariously through your players. >> Yep. Yep. Yep. Absolutely. Right, I think you hit you hit the nail nail on the head. Just just, you know, being able to to watch some of these kids grow up um into into young men and see their careers take off. Um and again, even with all this, right? I make sure parents are in the forefront. Like this still isn't about me. And there's right, course players invite me to everything. And I attend, don't get me wrong. I attend, but I still want to be in the background, you know, because you know, I feel like this is my job. I feel like this is my calling, even when I wasn't ready to accept it, but God had a plan for me and I know, you know, coaches and and again, I am in that that coaching world where, you know, I talk to other coaches or met, you know, certain clinics or whatever and right, I hear some of these other coaches stories like, "Listen, man, I was at this place for, you know, 20, 30 years. I never even made it in the playoffs. You know, I never even had an opportunity to coach in a state championship game. So, I know how how blessed I am and and again, this is not by accident because I have some amazing coaches around me. I do have some good great support system and again, I'm I'm I'm excited about not only where our program has come, but where it's going still. >> And and in closing, and thank you again for for spending some time talking about your career. >> Absolutely. >> Your son CJ is an ascending player for the Florida Gators basketball team. He's really fun to watch as I mentioned earlier in our conversation. What's your perspective on the growth that he's shown during his time and what's it like being a father, being able to watch him play? I'm I'm sure you're I'm sure you're very proud. >> Yeah. Yeah, very proud. Very proud. I I remember just walking into the arena and and he was warming up. I think the first game of the season against Arizona and they played out in Vegas. And my wife and I, we were like just walking out and we were coming out of the tunnel and he was right in the corner shooting a three. Right and just seeing the name on the back of his jersey. Like I had a moment. I had a moment because, right? He was a two-sport guy for the longest and he's so mature. I can remember when, right, he wanted to sit out to make the decision to just focus on one sport and which I thought that was huge of him, right? Because a lot of times, right, when your dad's the head coach, he was my quarterback. Of course, he won what? He won two state championships back-to-back as a sophomore and a junior. So, he didn't even play football his senior year. Right? So, for him to have that amount of pressure on him and it's not even on purpose. Like sometimes, right, just because of your last name, just because your dad might be the coach, just because, right, your dad had these accolades and you're trending to all this stuff, there's there's some pressure even when we say it's not. And for him to sit down and was like, "Yo, Dad, I just want to focus on on basketball." Right? I was I was happy for him, right? He He's He's always been super mature for his for his age. Uh but to see his [clears throat] growth, I I can remember just last year we went out to dinner. He was playing early um a lot and and you know, I wanted to just talk to him to see how he was feeling and like his confidence never wavered and he felt like, "Hey, Dad, I'm I'm on a national championship type of team with great players, right? I I know my opportunity will come." And just to see how the season went um by the end of the season he got more time and he performed well, right? And I know right there's and and then, you know, just the pressure he would have to, you know, encounter, you know, me being his father and then him also being the hometown kid at the University of Florida, right? Everyone knows him, right? Just think about the amount of high school games he's played in this area where people supported him, right? He can't even go into a store, but when I tell you he he handled him he handled himself well all the time, all the time. I'm extremely proud. Um, he'll have a big season this year. Right? Right now, I think just just looking at him he's still growing. Um, and and and he's having a really good off season already, so um, I'm excited to see him in year two. Uh, just by, you know, all of the flashes he was able to show in in year one, said a lot about his character and um, but he'll continue to grow. >> Well, I look forward to following along this season. There there's something that everyone can take from your story, Cornelius. Being able to battle through adversity, discover your passion and and really flourish is something that I think it is what everything is all about. And I I thank you for for sharing your story with us. >> Absolutely. Thanks for having me. >> Absolutely. Well, that's going to do it for this episode of the Cheko Daily. For Cornelius Ingram, I'm Andrew DeCheko. I'll catch you all on the next one. >> [music]

title: Football at Four: DiCecco's Updated Look at the NFC East
text: It's time for football at four with Andrew DiScepolo. We have a little NFC East mailbag questions today for Andrew. Thanks to everybody who submitted your questions for Andrew today. We had a good mailbag this week. This is the NFC East version for Andrew DiScepolo who joins us right now on the Sports Bash. Andrew, what's going on, man? >> Hey Mike, I'm doing great. Good to be with you. >> You got uh So you got A.J. Brown gone to Boston, Jaylen Brown coming to Philadelphia. It has been a massive day uh for the Philadelphia and New England fan bases again. Uh crazy stuff is happening, but people still getting ready for the start of training camp, which is less than a month to to go here. And uh we'll start with the question right down here in Wildwood. Brian in Wildwood wants to know, "Hey Andrew, uh pick your favorite NFC East quarterback. Who has the biggest year out of Hurts, Prescott, Daniels, or Darnold?" >> Well, my favorite NFC East quarterback has, you know, I'm going to say Jayden Daniels because I've liked He was my top-rated quarterback coming out of the draft a couple years ago, and I like his athleticism. He doesn't have the the frame to support the way that he plays, so you worry about longevity purposes, kind of like RG3. But I just like the way that he plays the position, and that dates back to court to his college years. Then I would have to say Jalen Hurts because Jalen Hurts is a player that when I was a senior draft analyst at at a certain outlet, when I had to write four players, four or five players that I thought were going to sneak into the first round, one of the players that I put in there was Jalen Hurts just because the winning pedigree, the the maturity that he always exhibited when he was there at Alabama or Oklahoma Oklahoma, and I I just I just thought that his skill set really translated to the NFL, and he was really fun to watch. >> All right, so he likes Jayden Daniels there. A lot of quarterback, you know, conversation I'm sure as we get closer here. Jackson Dart very intrigued by where he goes in year number two for the Giants. This question regards his receiver Malik Nabers. Before that injury, Andrew, did you see Nabers as a potential top five wide receiver in the league? >> Top five might be a little strong, but he was certainly trending in top eight the territory and I think a lot of questions are going to be surrounding Malik Nabers. How does he respond from the injury? But this is a player that he he looks the part. He wins his matchups routinely. I think he's going to continue to get better the more repetitions and the more experience he gets. The sky's really the limit for him. I don't know that you can really cap what he's able to do. He has the body type to be able to go up and get the football. He's really good route runner and he's explosive. So I I think really you're going to see him emerge return back to form this year, but I I I liked him quite a bit and he got off to a fast start. This one has to do with Washington and it's similar with Jayden Daniels here that now that Jayden Daniels is back, how much better do you think the Commanders will actually be this year? They had high expectations coming off of the NFC Championship game the year before. >> Yeah, they sure did. I don't know that I'm fully sold on the Commanders based off of roster construction, but as I mentioned, I I do like Jayden Daniels quite a bit. Now, I'm not saying I believe he's the best quarterback in the NFC East. I think Dak Prescott is, but my favorite to watch play the position has been Jayden Daniels and he does give them a much higher floor when he's available and you look at some of the pieces that they've added, some of the coaches that they've added. I I I believe that you're going to see a lot more structure with the organization. I think they're sort of a middling team right now. They're not quite ready, Mike, in my estimation to make a an dent in the NFC East. I think it's going to come down to Philadelphia and Dallas, but I do like some of the things that the Commanders have done and we'll see if they continue to trend in a positive direction with Jayden Daniels there uh, under center. >> Uh, another question for Andrew in our NFC East mailbag. This one has to do with the Giants about John Harball bringing instant culture. Last year the Giants fell apart in some fourth quarters. How much does Harball eliminate that? >> Well, I think adding someone like John Harball is ultimately going to have a dramatic effect in discipline and being able to close out games. I just don't know if the Giants have enough talent to be able to match that, but you are going to see a much more fundamentally sound team, one that should be able to close out games if they are in position to do so. And when you look at just the NFC East as a whole, I think John Harball was one of the biggest this off-season because it does add an element of stability and structure to a team that was sort of just haphazardly going by the wayside a little bit and they never really had a direction. You didn't you never really knew what the Giants were and there's not a lot you can do for injuries and I think you have to keep an eye on Cam Skaterboo and and Jackson Dart because of the way they play the game, but with John Harball at the helm there, that CEO coach that I know some may roll their eyes over, but I mean he's had a remarkable track record of success and I don't know that he's going to be able to to uplift the Giants to to prominence fully, but I I do believe you're going to see them make some some strides. >> All right, this one is from Stephen Lower Township. He said the Cowboys have all their offense back, but what about their defense? Is the defense any better than it was a year ago? >> It is. They've added some different pieces. They have Donovan as a Rocco, a Williamstown guy who's entering year two. Savon Rebel, the the cornerback who was injured for half of last season. He was a the out of East Carolina that I like quite a bit. I have the sense that Christian Parker will really like a player of of his of his makeup and be able to get the most out of that player. When you look at their offense, clearly, and as you outlined, the offense is not the problem. It was the defense surrendering leads and things of that nature. They've patched certain areas of that group that I think you're going to be able to see noticeable differences this year. And with Christian Parker there, and you know this, and I've spoken really highly of Christian Parker for a number of years now. I I have full confidence that he's going to have that defense trending in the right direction. And and some of the pieces that they've added, whether it be through the draft or free agency, certainly reflect Christian's vision, just having been around him for a couple of years, about what he looks for in certain players. So, you're going to see a defense that's much more consistent and much more disciplined, and as well as having better communication. >> All right. We're talking with Andrew Di Cecco. Our off-season summer mailbag continues. These are very NFC East focused today. We got some NFC East questions here. This one's on Washington and Terry McLaurin. Can the Commanders really count on Terry McLaurin to be the top a top guy anymore? >> I don't think so. I I I really like Terry McLaurin. I think he's more I've always viewed him as more of a of a two. And as a complimentary piece, he's been cast as the one, and he's had great success. I'm not taking anything away from him. But, you know, he's been banged up. He's a little bit older now. And and I think because of that, he I have my questions as to whether or not he can really, you know, take that top mantle as as as the the primary receiving you know, the receiving element of that of that offense. So, I'm not quite sold on it. He's a good player, not a great player. And if you have an offense that it runs through Terry McLaurin, I I think that, you know, you probably should have done some better roster management to make sure that that wouldn't be the case. But, >> Well, Andrew, they went and Go ahead. >> Go ahead. No, go ahead. They're still going to be consistent. They're still going to be He's still going to be able to get his numbers, but in terms of just being a number one wide receiver, you know, as as it's defined, I just have my questions of him being able to take over games as he has in the past. >> Well, yeah, I was going to add, you know, they changed their offensive coordinator there as well, Kingsbury. They had D'Eriq King there last year. He was kind of banged up. They never got to implement that there. So, I'm wondering what David Blough, how much there you know, we're talking about Philadelphia and the changes to their offense. What difference will the Washington offense have? I guess that remains to be seen. >> Yeah, I think you're going to see David Blough, who by the way was a quarterback at Purdue. You talk about Sean McVay and having a fast rise, David Blough is should be in that same category. I imagine you're going to see more detailed mechanics and you'll be able to tell the most noticeable difference as it pertains to Jayden Daniels and how he plays the position, just given David Blough's background. But in terms of what he's going to bring from an offensive standpoint, his philosophy, there's not a lot to go off of there, but that's that's also a reason to have some questions. He's unproven. He's not an established coordinator. So, until you really see it on the field, you really have no way of knowing what that offense is going to look like. I'm more so banking on Jayden Daniels being healthy and you saw the caliber of player that he is when he's healthy. Their offensive line's not that bad. I do like Terry McLaurin, although I like him more as a number two wide receiver at this stage of his career, but and they've added Chigoziem Okonkwo as a tight end in free agency, I believe, and he's a solid player. They've added some pieces. I just don't think that they're ready to contend for anything in in any meaningful way. >> All right, we'll ask I'll fit one more in here for Andrew. Andrew, the last time you mentioned Christian Parker, how much you like him for Dallas. But is their defense actually better now without Micah Parsons? >> Well, I mean they didn't have Micah Parsons last year and you're never going to be a better defense without someone like a Micah Parsons, but they've added pieces.
